tavily_results.title: Our regulatory business plan for 2026-2028 | National Energy System Operator
tavily_results.content:
Our energy system is complex, with an increasing number of interconnections. This means that disruption to one part can have implications for another. But this complexity also provides us with more options to mitigate problems.

We will develop comprehensive and independent insights across the entire energy system, offering clear recommendations to policy makers, industry decision makers and leadership across our organisation on how to accelerate energy transition progress.

Whether you’re interested in the innovation underway in the Markets team or are looking to brush up on market fundamentals, you’ve come to the right place. [...] Security of Supply analyses where the energy we need over the short, medium and long-term will come from. In doing so it assesses a wide range of factors that could affect our supply of energy, enabling early actions and decisions to ensure we can meet future demand.

From hospitals to households, telecoms to transportation, our society relies on electricity. Our control centre makes sure there is always a reliable and safe supply as we move megawatts around the country.

We will deliver efficient system access for Generation and Demand projects, so that those projects that are first ready can be first served – delivering the energy system to meet net zero and facilitating economic growth by connecting new and existing industries. [...] Under our regulatory framework, we must follow Ofgem’s guidance to produce business plans detailing how our activities deliver value for consumers. ​ The framework includes our requirements for performance reporting via our incentives scheme.​

Our regulatory framework includes; two licenses, our funding arrangements and regular performance monitoring and reporting requirements.

The requirements and obligations under our regulatory framework are set out in our licences, with further detail provided in both the Performance Arrangements Governance Document (PAGD)and the Business Plan Guidance.​

From 1 April 2026, we have moved onto our new enduring regulatory framework, which replaces the RIIO‑2 framework that concluded in March 2026. ​

local_documents.snippet: Environmental Burden of Disease from Coal-Fired Power Plants in Germany Environmental Burden of Disease from Coal-Fired Power Plants in Germany This study estimates the health burden in Germany caused by long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide and PM2.5 emissions from hard coal- and lignite-fired power plants in 2015. The authors focus on source-specific disease burden rather than total air pollution, asking how much disease could be attributed specifically to emissions from these coal power plants. The central conclusion is that both hard coal and lignite contributed a measurable burden of disease, with lignite producing the larger impact for both pollutants. The methodology combines air pollution modeling, population exposure assessment, and health burden calculation. local_documents.snippet: to Ambient PM2.5 Mortality This paper provides a global assessment of which sectors and fuels contribute most to ambient PM2.5 exposure and PM2.5-attributable mortality. The motivation is practical: fine particulate matter is the world's leading environmental health risk, but effective air quality policy requires knowing which sources drive the burden in different places. The study covers 21 world regions, 204 countries, and 200 sub-national areas, allowing comparison across global, national, and urban-relevant scales. The methodology combines atmospheric modeling, satellite-based exposure estimates, emissions inventories, and disease-specific health risk functions. The authors ran 24 sensitivity simulations with the GEOS-Chem global chemical transport model to estimate source and fuel contributions. local_documents.snippet: to reduce air pollution from all major sources, improve public health, protect the natural environment, and support cleaner economic growth. It begins from the position that the country has already reduced many of the worst pollution problems through regulation, industrial investment, and a cleaner energy mix, but that air pollution remains one of the UK's largest public health challenges. The strategy stresses that harmful emissions now come from many diffuse sources, not only from large factories or road traffic. The document identifies air pollution as a result of how the UK generates power, heats homes, produces food, manufactures goods, and moves people and freight. It focuses on five damaging pollutants covered by legally binding international reduction commitments: fine particulate matter, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, sulphur dioxide, and non-methane volatile organic compounds. local_documents.title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines
local_documents.snippet: ticles are recognized as important concerns, but the evidence was not sufficient to derive full quantitative air quality guideline values. WHO recommends monitoring, exposure assessment, source control where possible, and risk communication for these particle types. Implementation is presented as a policy process, not just a measurement exercise. Countries are encouraged to assess national needs and capacity, translate the guideline levels into enforceable standards where appropriate, build air quality management systems, and use health risk assessment to compare policy options. WHO stresses the role of the health sector in synthesizing evidence, communicating risks, monitoring impacts, and supporting decision-making, while also making clear that air pollution control requires cooperation across transport, energy, housing, industry, agriculture, urban planning, and environmental agencies
